red.focus: Learn why Palsgraf limited the duty of care despite a chain of injury.
red.summary: Railroad employees helped a passenger board a train, a concealed package fell, and an explosion injured a person some distance away. The New York Court of Appeals asked whether she was within the foreseeable zone of risk.
checklist: I can describe the accident and Palsgraf's position
I can explain Cardozo's duty reasoning
I can distinguish physical causation from legally recognized liability

sections.title: A surprising chain of events
sections.body_md: In Palsgraf v Long Island Railroad Co. (1928), railway employees assisted a man boarding a moving train. His package fell; it contained fireworks and exploded. The shock brought down weighing scales some distance away, injuring Helen Palsgraf. She had not been carrying the package and its dangerous contents were not apparent. The case shows why proving that events happened in a connected sequence does not settle whether the defendant owed this claimant a legal duty of care.
sections.audio_script: In Palsgraf v Long Island Railroad Co. (1928), railway employees assisted a man boarding a moving train. His package fell; it contained fireworks and exploded. The shock brought down weighing scales some distance away, injuring Helen Palsgraf. She had not been carrying the package and its dangerous contents were not apparent. The case shows why proving that events happened in a connected sequence does not settle whether the defendant owed this claimant a legal duty of care.

sections.title: The majority focused on foreseeable danger
sections.body_md: Chief Judge Benjamin Cardozo, writing for the majority of the New York Court of Appeals, concluded that the guards' conduct did not create a reasonably foreseeable risk of injury to Palsgraf in the relevant circumstances. Without a duty owed to her in relation to that risk, negligence liability could not be established by tracing the physical chain backward. The judgment was not a claim that her injuries were imaginary. It identified a limit on which consequences the defendant could legally be held responsible for.

The judgment was not a claim that her injuries were imaginary. It identified a limit on which consequences the defendant could legally be held responsible for.

sections.title: Separate injury, cause, and duty
sections.body_md: An injured person deserves attention, but a civil court must also apply the boundaries of legal responsibility. Write the events in order, then separately ask whether the defendant's conduct created a foreseeable risk to this person. That test came from this court and period; it is not an identical rule governing all countries. The beginner's essential lesson is that a harmful consequence and a defendant's involvement are necessary subjects of inquiry, not automatically a complete negligence claim.

yellow.focus: Analyze the split between Cardozo and Andrews in Palsgraf.
yellow.summary: The Palsgraf majority and dissent disagreed on where negligence law should limit responsibility. Compare plaintiff-relative duty with broader duty and proximate-cause reasoning.
checklist: I can explain Cardozo's plaintiff-relative duty approach
I can summarize Andrews's dissent fairly
I can identify the legal function of proximate cause

sections.title: Cardozo begins with the claimant
sections.body_md: For the majority, the negligent character of an act is relational: the defendant must have exposed a person in the relevant position to a foreseeable risk. Since the guards' conduct presented no apparent threat to Palsgraf from the concealed package, the court found no relevant duty owed to her. The majority placed the limit early in the negligence analysis. A claimant's real injury and the guards' participation were not enough to establish legal responsibility.
sections.audio_script: For the majority, the negligent character of an act is relational: the defendant must have exposed a person in the relevant position to a foreseeable risk. Since the guards' conduct presented no apparent threat to Palsgraf from the concealed package, the court found no relevant duty owed to her. The majority placed the limit early in the negligence analysis. A claimant's real injury and the guards' participation were not enough to establish legal responsibility.

sections.title: Andrews locates the limit differently
sections.body_md: Judge William Andrews dissented. His approach treated the duty to exercise due care more broadly and placed greater emphasis on whether the injury was proximately connected to the negligent conduct. He saw the causation issue as a matter of practical judgment about the consequences sufficiently related to an act. The dissent did not insist on liability for every remote event. The disagreement was about the doctrinal location and formulation of limits, not whether any limit should exist.

sections.title: Two theories, one problem
sections.body_md: Imagine a careless act creating risk to a nearby passenger, followed by an unexpected chain injuring someone farther away. Cardozo's approach first considers whether the particular claimant fell within the range of foreseeable risk. Andrews's reasoning would examine the broader duty and then the appropriate limit on causal responsibility. Neither method replaces the need for reliable evidence or for a governing legal rule. Explain which theory applies in the jurisdiction rather than blending the two into a vague idea of fairness.

orange.focus: Use Caparo and Robinson to understand modern limits on English duty of care.
orange.summary: Caparo rejected a broad auditor duty to a share purchaser who relied on published accounts. Robinson later cautioned against treating Caparo's three considerations as a universal test that replaces established negligence duties.
checklist: I can state why the claimed auditor duty failed in Caparo
I can describe the role and limits of Caparo considerations
I can apply Robinson's ordinary-negligence analysis to positive police acts

sections.title: Financial reliance does not always create a duty
sections.body_md: In Caparo Industries plc v Dickman (1990), Caparo alleged that it relied on inaccurate audited accounts when acquiring shares in a company. The House of Lords did not recognize the asserted duty of care owed by the auditors to Caparo for that investment purpose. The context and purpose of preparing statutory accounts mattered. The judgment reflected concern with proximity and whether imposing such responsibility was fair, just, and reasonable, not a declaration that accountants could never owe anyone a duty.
sections.audio_script: In Caparo Industries plc v Dickman (1990), Caparo alleged that it relied on inaccurate audited accounts when acquiring shares in a company. The House of Lords did not recognize the asserted duty of care owed by the auditors to Caparo for that investment purpose. The context and purpose of preparing statutory accounts mattered. The judgment reflected concern with proximity and whether imposing such responsibility was fair, just, and reasonable, not a declaration that accountants could never owe anyone a duty.

sections.title: A framework can become oversimplified
sections.body_md: Caparo became associated with foreseeability, proximity, and whether imposing a duty would be fair, just, and reasonable. Courts should not treat those words as a complete algorithm for every negligence dispute. Existing categories and incremental development are important. In Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police (2018), the U.K. Supreme Court stressed that Caparo was not a universal three-stage test to be applied mechanically whenever duty arises. The correct starting point often is established law concerning the particular relationship and conduct.

The correct starting point often is established law concerning the particular relationship and conduct.

sections.title: Police are not generally immune from negligent acts
sections.body_md: Robinson involved an older pedestrian injured when police officers physically struggled with a suspect during an arrest. The Supreme Court rejected an assumed blanket immunity and analyzed whether ordinary negligence principles applied to the officers' positive conduct. This does not create unlimited police liability for failing to prevent all crime. It distinguishes harm allegedly caused by officials' own acts from attempts to make them answer for every danger created by others. A master's analysis must name that distinction and test the facts, not rely on a slogan.

black.focus: Defend duty limits that do not erase meaningful protection against harm.
black.summary: Palsgraf, Caparo, and Robinson reveal that limits on liability can be principled or arbitrarily exclusionary. Critique how courts draw boundaries around foreseeable risk, economic dependence, and the acts of public officials.
checklist: I can compare relational and institutional theories of duty
I can identify policy risks in unlimited and overrestricted liability
I can propose evidence-sensitive boundaries for modern hazards

sections.title: Liability is not identical to sympathy
sections.body_md: A person can suffer devastating injury without having a legally actionable negligence claim against every actor connected to the event. Palsgraf limits duty by a foreseeable relationship to risk. Caparo concerns the scope and purpose of an auditor's obligations in a financial context. Robinson shows that caution about imposing novel duties does not justify a sweeping exemption for officials who negligently injure someone by their own actions. These cases ask different questions; a doctoral account must not turn them into one generalized anti-claimant rule.
sections.audio_script: A person can suffer devastating injury without having a legally actionable negligence claim against every actor connected to the event. Palsgraf limits duty by a foreseeable relationship to risk. Caparo concerns the scope and purpose of an auditor's obligations in a financial context. Robinson shows that caution about imposing novel duties does not justify a sweeping exemption for officials who negligently injure someone by their own actions. These cases ask different questions; a doctoral account must not turn them into one generalized anti-claimant rule.

sections.title: Rules can encourage safety or prevent redress
sections.body_md: Overly broad liability may expose professionals to indeterminate claims and distort activities benefiting others. Overly narrow duty rules can leave injured persons without remedy even when preventable harm occurred. Analyze who could foresee and control the risk, who relied on whom, which safeguards existed, and whether the legal system offers another effective remedy. Reject both the claim that any severe injury demands damages and the view that institutional status should provide immunity from ordinary care standards.

sections.title: Design boundaries for connected technology
sections.body_md: Imagine a software auditor publishes a security assessment relied on by unknown downstream users, while a public agency deploys the product and causes direct harm. A precise theory would separate professional assumption of responsibility, foreseeable class of claimants, economic versus physical loss, and the agency's positive conduct. Determine the applicable jurisdiction and established duty categories before proposing reform. Legitimate limits should make responsibility predictable and fair while preserving meaningful protection for those whose lives are affected.
